title: Dawud and the two brothers
hookLine: two men climb the wall with a dispute over ewes, and Dawud realizes he was tested and repents (38:21–25)

lines: TWO MEN COME OVER THE WALL.
DON'T BE AFRAID: JUDGE BETWEEN US.
cards: It's a private hour. Dawud is in his prayer chamber, and the commentators say no one was to come in. Then two men come over the wall.
Not through the door. Over the wall. He's startled; the text says he was afraid.
They say, quickly: don't be afraid. We're two parties in a dispute; one of us has wronged the other. Judge between us with truth, don't be unjust, and guide us to the right path.
Then one of them tells his story, and Dawud answers before the text gives the other one a word.

teach.b: Surah Sad, verse twenty-three. The first man says: this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe.
And he said, give it to me, and he overpowered me in argument. Ninety-nine and one. And Dawud says, right away: he has wronged you by asking to add your ewe to his.
Many partners wrong one another, except those who believe and do good, and how few they are. Then verse twenty-four, the turn. Dawud realized that We had tested him.
He asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down bowing, and turned back in repentance. What was the test? The Qur'an doesn't say, and commentators differ.

Some later stories, known as Isra'iliyyat, tie it to an episode about another man's wife; many Muslim scholars, Ibn Kathir among them, set those stories aside, holding that prophets are protected from such a sin.

teach.h: HE RULED BEFORE THE OTHER SPOKE.
teach.b: A reading many find more convincing stays inside the scene: Dawud ruled after hearing only one side.

teach.h: HE KNEW HE WAS TESTED, AND BOWED.
teach.b: The text never gives the second man a word. The story was built to make him judge fast, and he did. And the moment he saw it, he didn't defend himself.
He went down on his face.
Verse twenty-six gives the lesson to him directly: O Dawud, We have made you a successor on earth, so judge between people with truth, and don't follow desire.
Many Muslims prostrate when they recite verse twenty-four; a hadith in Bukhari reports that Ibn 'Abbas saw the Prophet ﷺ prostrate there.

how: Many Muslims perform a prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilawa) at 38:24; schools differ on whether it is required or recommended, and Islamic legal teaching stresses hearing both parties before judging.

o: a trial that shows what's inside a person
a dispute between two brothers over sheep
a sin that can never be forgiven by God

games.q: the dispute over the wall — tap the pairs.
p: he knew he was tested, and bowed

s: the Qur'an spells out exactly what Dawud's test was
it doesn't; commentators differ, and many reject the later stories.
Dawud ruled before the second man spoke
he answered right after the first man's story.
many Muslims prostrate when reciting this passage
a hadith in Bukhari says the Prophet prostrated at it.

games.q: you're Dawud. a man tells you his brother has ninety-nine ewes and wants his only one. the brother hasn't spoken yet. what do you do?
o: rule for the man with one ewe.
ask the brother for his side.
games.why: Dawud ruled at once, then realized he'd been tested, asked forgiveness and bowed. many read the test as judging after one side.

practice: Bring to mind one recent judgment, about a coworker, a relative, someone online, where you heard one side and decided. Now give the other side a voice: what might they say, if they got to speak?
You don't have to change your mind; just let the second man talk, and notice how it feels to hold the judgment a little more loosely.

wordCard.voice: Fitna, the trial that shows what's inside, the word behind Dawud's test after he ruled too quickly on the two brothers' dispute. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: We tested him (38:24), from fitna, a trial that shows what's inside.

carryVoice: Your line: judge, then look at yourself. Ninety-nine ewes, one ewe, and a second man who never spoke. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Tafsir Ibn Kathir on 38:21–25 (caution about Isra'iliyyat)
